title: 2027 Outlook: Build Resilience Into Portfolio Returns
summary: Learn how a resilient real estate portfolio can protect cash flow, reduce volatility, and support stronger long-term returns.
body_markdown:
As you evaluate[portfolio performance](https://www.cbiz.com/insights/article/real-estate-noi-in-2027-build-cash-flow-that-holds-up) heading into 2027, risks once outside financial planning may now shape cash flow, financing flexibility, asset value, and long-term returns.


This shift may change how you evaluate resilience. Properties don’t need to suffer catastrophic damage for risk to reduce returns. Coverage gaps, retained losses, technology failures, tenant disruption, lender requirements, and regulatory obligations can pressure NOI and liquidity before a physical loss occurs.


The key question isn’t whether to manage risk, but whether you are evaluating it early enough to guide major investment and portfolio decisions.


## Risk Has Become a Financial Variable


[Real estate](https://www.cbiz.com/industries/real-estate) has always balanced risk and return. For owners preparing for 2027, that relationship is becoming more immediate as insurance, operational, cyber, compliance, valuation, and financing risks increasingly influence investment performance.


Recent research highlights the importance of this connection. A[Federal Reserve analysis](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/rising-property-insurance-costs-and-pass-through-to-rents-for-apartment-buildings-20250919.html) of CMBS-financed apartment properties found that average monthly insurance costs rose from $39 per unit in 2019 to $68 in 2024, with each $1 increase in insurance expense associated with roughly $0.74 less net income. This demonstrates how insurance volatility can move directly through the income statement.


Even if market pricing improves, the premium alone doesn’t provide the full picture. Owners need to understand what their coverage truly protects and where exposures remain.


Insurance is only one example. More broadly, risks once managed independently are now shaping financial performance, investment decisions, and the assumptions owners use to plan for growth or protect value.


Financing risk can also emerge when insurance programs no longer align with lender requirements. As lenders scrutinize coverage limits, exclusions, deductibles, and catastrophe exposure more closely, owners may discover during renewal that their coverage does not satisfy loan covenants. That can create last-minute disruption, delay financing decisions, or lead to force-placed coverage, which is often significantly more expensive than coverage secured directly by the property owner.


Individually, each of these exposures may seem manageable. Together, they can materially influence portfolio performance.


## The Hidden Cost of Looking at Risk in Silos


A key challenge for real estate leaders is evaluating risk in isolation. Insurance, cybersecurity, operations, compliance, valuation, and financing may each be managed effectively, but the portfolio experiences their effects together.


For example, rising insurance costs can pressure NOI and limit flexibility in valuation, refinancing, and reinvestment. Technology outages, vendor disruptions, regulatory obligations, or outdated valuation assumptions can have similar effects if reviewed only within a single function.


Contractual risk transfer deserves the same level of scrutiny. Lease agreements, subcontractor agreements, and property management arrangements can determine whether certain exposures remain with the property owner or are shifted to downstream parties. This is especially important when tenants or vendors create elevated exposure, such as warehouse or retail tenants, roofing contractors, or snow and ice removal providers whose work could affect employee, visitor, or property safety.


An integrated approach helps identify where risk may affect performance and where targeted investments, contract reviews, or insurance placement decisions can protect value. Rather than focusing solely on current NOI, consider how risk could influence cash flow assumptions, capital requirements, credit risk, transaction readiness, and exit strategy during the hold period.


## The Most Resilient Portfolios Are Built Before They Are Tested


Resilience is often seen as the ability to recover after disruption. However, the strongest portfolios are designed to withstand pressure before being tested.


This requires looking beyond immediate risk transfer to how the portfolio is structured, valued, financed, and operated. A resilient portfolio does not eliminate uncertainty, but it can help absorb disruption, maintain flexibility, and support better-informed decisions.


In practice, this may require stronger insurance reviews, closer coordination with lenders, greater scrutiny of lease and subcontractor terms, improved visibility into climate exposure, stronger cybersecurity controls, disciplined reserve planning, business continuity planning, and regular reviews of valuation and financing assumptions. The goal isn’t to evaluate every risk in isolation, but to identify which exposures could alter cash flow, limit flexibility, or change the investment case.


## Questions Real Estate Leaders Should Be Asking


With the 2027 outlook in mind, the most useful questions are practical:


**What return does the property generate after accounting for retained risks?**
This encourages looking beyond current NOI to consider coverage gaps, downtime, and capital needs that may pressure future cash flow.


**How might rising insurance costs and lender requirements affect future asset performance?**
Premium increases can squeeze operating margins, while stricter lender expectations around coverage, deductibles, exclusions, and catastrophe exposure can affect renewal timing, refinancing flexibility, and borrowing costs.


**Are leases, subcontractor agreements, and property management arrangements transferring risk effectively?**
Contractual insurance requirements, indemnification language, and coordination of coverage can help prevent avoidable exposures from remaining at the ownership level.


**Are climate and catastrophe exposures considered in long-term planning?**
Understanding these exposures can inform reserve planning, acquisition evaluation, and prioritization of capital projects to strengthen long-term performance.


**Would an operational disruption significantly affect cash flow?**
Business continuity planning is increasingly important as owners depend on connected systems and third-party partners for efficient operations.


**Are risk assumptions reflected in the valuation model?**
Expense growth, downtime, capital needs, credit risk, exit assumptions, and refinancing exposure can shape valuation and the owner’s flexibility to transact or hold.


**Could regulatory requirements change capital needs during the hold period?**
Jurisdictional requirements increasingly influence acquisition, asset management, and disposition planning. For example,[New York City Local Law 97](https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/codes/ll97-greenhouse-gas-emissions-reductions.page) applies to most buildings over 25,000 square feet and includes penalties tied to emissions above applicable limits.


## Resilience Belongs in the Underwriting Conversation


As investors evaluate opportunities and existing holdings in 2027, resilience is becoming integral to underwriting. Understanding how operational, financial, technology, and physical risks may shape performance can help owners make more informed portfolio decisions and maintain flexibility as market conditions change. To discuss how these issues may impact your real estate portfolio, contact amember of our team .


#### Frequently Asked Questions


Start by connecting risk review to financial planning, not treating it as a separate exercise. Owners may want to assess how insurance costs, retained losses, lender requirements, lease terms, technology dependence, reserve planning, and regulatory obligations could affect cash flow, refinancing options, capital needs, and exit strategy.


Coverage terms can influence more than annual expense. If limits, deductibles, exclusions, or catastrophe exposure do not align with lender expectations or asset-level risk, owners could face renewal challenges, higher borrowing costs, force-placed coverage, or assumptions that no longer reflect the property’s true risk profile.


Contract language can determine whether certain exposures remain with the owner or are shifted to tenants, vendors, contractors, or property managers. Reviewing insurance requirements, indemnification provisions, and coverage coordination can help reduce avoidable retained risk and support more predictable performance during the hold period.
